title: Provided, That This Limitation Shall Not Apply: the Carve-Out Inside the Statute That Killed TIA

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: No money figure is public here, which is itself the point: the carve-out's funding is "expressly provided in the National Foreign Intelligence Program", an account whose amounts are not in the public law. The statute appropriates to a programme it does not describe, by reference to a document it does not publish.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise is a semicolon's worth of drafting. Subsection (a) opens with the widest possible prohibition — "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, none of the funds appropriated or otherwise made available in this or any other Act may be obligated for the Terrorism Information Awareness Program" — and then continues: "Provided, That this limitation shall not apply to the program hereby authorized for Processing, analysis, and collaboration tools for counterterrorism foreign intelligence, as described in the Classified Annex". The prohibition and its exception are one sentence.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is statutory, not rhetorical. The exempted programme is identified only by a generic description — "Processing, analysis, and collaboration tools" — and defined "as described in the Classified Annex accompanying the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2004". A reader of the public law cannot establish what was exempted, who built it, or what it cost. Four months earlier the Department had been compelled to tell Congress, in the open, that TIA was a portfolio of separately named component programmes — Genisys, EELD, SSNA, HumanID, ARM, NGFR and others — which is what makes a carve-out defined by function rather than by name operable.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: What the proviso confers is not a contract but a condition: a line of work survives the prohibition that was written to end it, inside an account with no public line items, with its scope limited by subsection (b) to "lawful military operations of the United States conducted outside the United States" or "lawful foreign intelligence activities conducted wholly overseas, or wholly against non-United States citizens". Who received the money, and whether that limit held, is not in this document and is not asserted.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The whitewash is the public closure itself. The programme was terminated by name, in a statute, in language absolute on its face, and reported as such; and in the same section Congress wrote the exception. Subsection (c) then defines the banned programme to include "any successor program, funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or any other Department or element of the Federal Government, including the individual components of such Program" — closing the successor loophole with one hand while the proviso opens one with the other.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A statutory disclosure duty that had already forced the programme into the open: Pub. L. 108-7, Division M, § 111(b), under which the Department filed its "Report to Congress regarding the Terrorism Information Awareness Program" on 20 May 2003, naming the component programmes.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A drafting pattern: terminate a named programme in public law, and preserve its function through a proviso referring to a classified annex and a different appropriations account. The termination is citable; the continuation is not.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Public exposure forces a statutory ban; the ban's own proviso moves the capability into the classified annex; the annex is not reviewable, so the next exposure concerns a successor that cannot be described; and subsection (c)'s prohibition on "any successor program" cannot bite on what subsection (a) has already exempted.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Total Information Awareness was never really cancelled — that Congress pretended to kill it while quietly handing the whole thing to Palantir and the intelligence agencies.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Half of it is in the statute and half of it is not, and the division matters. THE PART THAT IS IN THE STATUTE: § 8131(a) of Public Law 108-87 bans funding for the Terrorism Information Awareness Program "in this or any other Act" and then exempts, in the same sentence, "the program hereby authorized for Processing, analysis, and collaboration tools for counterterrorism foreign intelligence, as described in the Classified Annex", funded through the National Foreign Intelligence Program. That is not an inference, a leak or a theory; it is the enacted text at 117 Stat. 1102–1103, and anyone can read it. The claim that the cancellation was accompanied by a preserved carve-out is simply true. THE PART THAT IS NOT: no company is named anywhere in § 8131. The words "Palantir", "contractor" and "vendor" do not appear in it. The statute does not say what the Classified Annex describes, who was paid, whether any component of TIA in fact continued, or whether subsection (b)'s limitation to overseas operations and non-US persons was observed. The node's original title asserted a Palantir enclosure; nothing read for this dossier establishes any connection between this statute and that company, and the dossier therefore asserts none. A SECOND LIMIT, on provenance: the DARPA report to Congress was read from a copy hosted by the Electronic Privacy Information Center, an advocacy organisation, because no government-hosted copy was located. Its cover page and contents are internally consistent with the filed original, but that was not verified by comparison.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Section 8131 of the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2004, Public Law 108-87, 30 September 2003, at 117 Stat. 1102–1103. Subsection (a) prohibits obligating funds appropriated in that or any other Act for the Terrorism Information Awareness Program, with a proviso exempting the programme authorised for "Processing, analysis, and collaboration tools for counterterrorism foreign intelligence" as described in the Classified Annex to the same Act, funded in the National Foreign Intelligence Program. Subsection (b) restricts funds for that programme to lawful US military operations conducted outside the United States, or lawful foreign intelligence activities conducted wholly overseas or wholly against non-United States citizens. Subsection (c) defines the prohibited programme as Terrorism Information Awareness or Total Information Awareness "or any successor program" funded by DARPA or any other federal department or element, including the Program's individual components as developed by DARPA. Separately, the Department's statutorily compelled "Report to Congress regarding the Terrorism Information Awareness Program — Detailed Information" of 20 May 2003, filed under Pub. L. 108-7, Division M, § 111(b), sets out TIA as a portfolio of separately named component research programmes including Genisys, Genisys Privacy Protection, Evidence Extraction and Link Discovery, Scalable Social Network Analysis, MisInformation Detection, Human Identification at a Distance, Activity Recognition and Monitoring, and Next-Generation Face Technology, with sections on efficacy, legal framework, and impact on privacy and civil liberties.

citations.title: Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2004, Public Law 108-87, § 8131, 117 Stat. 1102–1103 (30 September 2003)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo.gov (255 KB) and read as extracted text; § 8131 appears at 117 Stat. 1102–1103. THIS IS THE STATUTE THAT IS ROUTINELY DESCRIBED AS HAVING KILLED TOTAL INFORMATION AWARENESS, AND IT CONTAINS ITS OWN EXCEPTION IN THE SAME SENTENCE. Subsection (a) in full: "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, none of the funds appropriated or otherwise made available in this or any other Act may be obligated for the Terrorism Information Awareness Program: Provided, That this limitation shall not apply to the program hereby authorized for Processing, analysis, and collaboration tools for counterterrorism foreign intelligence, as described in the Classified Annex accompanying the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2004, for which funds are expressly provided in the National Foreign Intelligence Program for counterterrorism foreign intelligence purposes." So the prohibition is absolute on its face — "this or any other Act" — and the proviso carves out a successor line of work whose description is not in the public law at all but in a Classified Annex, funded through a different account. Subsection (b) limits that carve-out: "None of the funds provided for Processing, analysis, and collaboration tools for counterterrorism foreign intelligence shall be available for deployment or implementation except for: (1) lawful military operations of the United States conducted outside the United States; or (2) lawful foreign intelligence activities conducted wholly overseas, or wholly against non-United States citizens." Subsection (c) then defines the banned program as broadly as the drafters could manage: "the term ``Terrorism Information Awareness Program'' means the program known either as Terrorism Information Awareness or Total Information Awareness, or any successor program, funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or any other Department or element of the Federal Government, including the individual components of such Program developed by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency." The two halves sit against each other in the same section: (c) reaches "any successor program" anywhere in the federal government, while (a)'s proviso exempts one by name from the only prohibition that would have bound it. WHAT IS NOT IN THE STATUTE: no company is named anywhere in § 8131. The words "Palantir", "contractor" and "vendor" do not appear in it. Nothing in this document identifies who received any money under the proviso, what the Classified Annex describes, or whether any component of TIA in fact continued. This citation establishes the shape of the loophole as enacted, and nothing about its use.

citations.title: Department of Defense / DARPA, "Report to Congress regarding the Terrorism Information Awareness Program — Detailed Information", in response to Consolidated Appropriations Resolution, 2003, Pub. L. No. 108-7, Division M, § 111(b), 20 May 2003
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded (1.35 MB) and read as extracted text. ON PROVENANCE, STATED PLAINLY: this is a copy of a Department of Defense report to Congress hosted by the Electronic Privacy Information Center, an advocacy organisation, not by a government domain. It carries the report's own cover page — "Report to Congress regarding the Terrorism Information Awareness Program / In response to Consolidated Appropriations Resolution, 2003, Pub. L. No. 108-7, Division M, § 111(b) / Detailed Information / May 20, 2003" — and its contents are internally consistent with that, but no government-hosted copy was located and opened, so the possibility that this file differs from the filed original has not been excluded by comparison. WHAT THE REPORT IS: a statutorily compelled disclosure, written four months before the programme was defunded, setting out the Information Awareness Office's component programmes by name and describing their purpose, efficacy and privacy implications. Its table of contents lists, as TIA and "High-Interest TIA-Related" programmes: Terrorism Information Awareness (TIA), Genisys, Genisys Privacy Protection, Evidence Extraction and Link Discovery (EELD), Scalable Social Network Analysis (SSNA), MisInformation Detection (MInDet), Human Identification at a Distance (HumanID), Activity, Recognition and Monitoring (ARM), and Next-Generation Face Technology (NGFR). It then has sections on "TIA Efficacy", "Measuring TIA Progress and Effectiveness", "Status of Component Research", "Laws and Regulations Governing Federal Government Information Collection", and "TIA's Impact on Privacy and Civil Liberties, and Recommended Practices, Procedures, Regulations or Legislation for TIA Deployment and Implementation to Eliminate or Minimize Adverse Effects". THE REASON IT IS CITED HERE: it establishes, on the record and by the government's own hand, that TIA was not one system but a named portfolio of separable component research programmes — which is what makes the later statutory language about "the individual components of such Program" and about a carve-out for "Processing, analysis, and collaboration tools" legible as something other than a drafting accident. WHAT IS NOT CITED FROM IT: no claim is made here about any component's capability, status or eventual disposition, and no company is named. Beyond the structure described above, the body of the report has not been mined for this dossier.
